content: Celery, scientifically known as Apium graveolens, is a plant species belonging to the family Apiaceae. It produces two significant vegetables: celery (the stalk) and celeriac (the root). Various cultivars of this species have been utilized for centuries, while some have only been domesticated in the last 200-300 years. Common Names Celery is known by different names across languages: English: celery, leaf celery, stalk celery, celeriac, turnip-rooted celery Spanish: apio French: céleri, céleri feuille, céleri à couper, céleri-branche, céleri à côtes, céleri-rave German: Sellerie Italian: Sedano Portuguese: aipo, salsão Russian: Сельдерей Chinese (Pinyin): qín cài (芹菜) Persian: کرفس Hindi: Radhuni, Ajwain Finnish: Selleri Norwegian: selleri Polish: seler Greek: Σέλινο Slovene: Zelena Swahili: Dania Uses Celery is widely consumed globally as a vegetable, either for its crisp stalks or its fleshy taproot. In temperate regions, celery is also cultivated for its seeds, which are a source of a valuable volatile oil used in the perfume and pharmaceutical industries. Celery seeds can be used as a spice or flavoring, either whole or ground and mixed with salt to create celery salt. Celery salt can also be derived from root extracts. It is commonly used as a seasoning, in cocktails (notably to enhance the flavor of Bloody Mary cocktails), on Chicago-style hot dogs, and in Old Bay Seasoning. Celery is a key ingredient in Louisiana Creole and Cajun cuisine, forming part of the holy trinity alongside onions and bell peppers. It is also one of the three vegetables (along with onions and carrots) that make up the French mirepoix, a foundational base for sauces and soups. Medicinal Uses The medicinal use of celery dates back to ancient times. Aulus Cornelius Celsus, around 30 AD, described the use of celery seeds in pills for pain relief. The entire plant is considered mildly stimulant, nourishing, and restorative. Celery juice can be consumed to alleviate joint and urinary tract inflammations, such as rheumatoid arthritis, cystitis, or urethritis. It is also used for conditions of weakness and nervous exhaustion. Celery seeds, harvested after the plant flowers in its second year, are the basis for a homeopathic extract used as a diuretic. This extract is believed to help eliminate toxins from the body, making it particularly beneficial for conditions like gout (where uric acid crystals accumulate in the joints) and arthritis. The seeds are also used as a mild digestive stimulant. The extract can be combined with almond or sunflower oil and massaged into arthritic joints or areas affected by gout, such as the feet or toes. The root of celery is an effective diuretic and has been used to treat urinary stones and gravel. It also acts as a bitter digestive remedy and liver stimulant. A tincture made from celery can be used as a diuretic for hypertension and urinary disorders, as a component in arthritis remedies, or as a kidney energy stimulant and cleanser. Ethnomedically, celery roots, seeds, and aerial parts are used to treat mild anxiety, agitation, loss of appetite, fatigue, cough, and as an anthelmintic (vermifuge). Caution The compound bergapten in celery seeds can increase photosensitivity, so the essential oil should not be applied externally in bright sunlight. The oil and large doses of seeds should be avoided during pregnancy, as they may act as a uterine stimulant. Seeds intended for cultivation are not suitable for consumption, as they are often treated with fungicides. Allergic Responses While celery is enjoyed by many, a small minority of individuals can experience severe allergic reactions. For those with celery allergies, exposure can lead to potentially fatal anaphylactic shock. The allergen in celery is not destroyed by cooking. Celery root (commonly consumed as celeriac or used in drinks) contains more allergen than the stalk, and the seeds have the highest allergen content. Celery is among a small group of foods, alongside peanuts, that provoke the most severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis). Allergic reactions can also occur from consuming foods processed with machinery that previously handled celery, making avoidance challenging. Celery allergy is most prevalent in Central Europe, contrasting with peanut allergy, which is more common in the United States. History Celery has a long history of use. Celery leaves and inflorescences were found in the garlands of Tutankhamun's tomb in ancient Egypt. Celery mericarps dating to the 7th century BC were discovered in the Heraion of Samos. However, it is unclear whether these remains represent wild or cultivated forms, as Apium graveolens grows wild in these areas. In Homer’s Iliad, the horses of the Myrmidons graze on wild celery in the marshes of Troy, and in the Odyssey, wild celery is mentioned in the meadows surrounding Calypso’s cave. In classical Greece, celery leaves were used as garlands for the dead, and the winners of the Isthmian Games were initially crowned with celery wreaths before being replaced by pine crowns. In Nemea, winners of sacred contests also wore celery garlands. Cultivation Apium graveolens grows up to 1 meter tall. Its leaves are pinnate to bipinnate, with rhombic leaflets measuring 3-6 cm long and 2-4 cm wide. The flowers are creamy-white, 2-3 mm in diameter, and produced in dense compound umbels. In North America, commercial celery production is dominated by the Pascal variety. Gardeners can grow various cultivars, many of which differ little from the wild species, primarily in having stouter leaf stems. These cultivars are classified as white or red, with white cultivars generally being the most flavorful, crisp, and tender. The wild form of celery, known as smallage, has a furrowed stalk with wedge-shaped leaves and a coarse, rank taste with a peculiar smell. Through cultivation and blanching, the stalks lose their acidic qualities and develop the mild, sweetish, aromatic taste characteristic of celery as a salad plant. Celery plants are raised from seeds, sown in hotbeds or open gardens depending on the season. After thinning and transplanting, they are planted in deep trenches for blanching, achieved by earthing up to exclude light from the stems. Historically, celery was grown as a winter and early spring vegetable. Due to its antitoxic properties, it was considered a cleansing tonic, welcomed after the stagnation of winter. Trivia Celery contains androsterone, a hormone released through sweat glands, said to attract women. There is a belief that celery has negative calories because digestion burns more calories than the vegetable provides. While this is technically true, the effect is negligible at only 6 kcal per rib. Celery is valuable in diets for its low-calorie fiber bulk. The Kalamazoo Celery Pickers were a minor league baseball team in the early 20th century. Dr. Brown’s produces a celery-flavored soft drink called Cel-Ray. Some pet rabbits consume large amounts of celery, but their natural gut flora allows them to digest the cellulose effectively. Exercise-induced anaphylaxis can be exacerbated by eating celery. In the British science fiction series Doctor Who, the Fifth Doctor wore a piece of celery on his lapel as a detector for certain gases. The closely related Apium bermejoi from Minorca is one of Europe’s rarest plants, with only 60 individuals remaining. The edible celery stalk is not a plant stem but a petiole, part of a leaf. Foley artists use celery stalks to simulate the sound of breaking bones. Celery was banned from Gillingham’s Priestfield Stadium in 1996 after a goalkeeper complained of being struck by celery thrown by spectators. Some people report numbness in their mouths after eating raw celery, possibly due to an allergic reaction. Ancient Greeks believed that those who disliked celery also disliked life. Fans of Chelsea Football Club have a chant involving celery, humorously suggesting its use in tickling. In the children’s show The Wonder Pets, celery is used as a celebratory treat. In the Honor Harrington book series, extraterrestrial treecats are addicted to celery. Celeryville, a small farming community in Ohio, was once known for its large celery yields.
